CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Carrots — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches counting to three with the crunchiest vegetable on the tray — and the rabbit story that makes every crunch louder.

What is this?

A carrot is an orange root vegetable that grows underground, pointy end down, leafy top up. It is sweet for a vegetable, which is why it is usually the first one children accept.

What does it mean?

Count the carrots is a three-count with a built-in reward: each counted carrot can be a crunched carrot. Counting with sound — snap, snap, snap — sticks better than counting in silence.

What does the child need to know?

Three is the target, not ten. A child who counts one-two-three and eats three carrots has completed a full math-and-snack cycle; extension can wait for tomorrow.

Why this matters

Carrots ride in every lunchbox and every soup — the word and the count rehearse together for years after this lesson.

What it teaches

Counting to three, loud chewing confidence, and the color orange.

Words to learn

carrotsthreeorangecrunchrabbittop

Say this to your child

“Count with me — one... two... three carrots! Rabbits eat carrots — can you crunch like a rabbit? Nibble nibble! Now hop! One hop for each carrot — hop, hop, hop!”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and count the carrots slowly — one, two, three — touching each one. Make the rabbit connection: carrots are what rabbits crunch. Then line up three real carrot rounds and count them onto the plate, eating one per number. Finish by hopping once for each carrot — three hops, three carrots, one proud rabbit.

Look closer at the picture

Watch whether the count and the touch stay together — if the finger races ahead of the words, slow the whole game down and count at finger speed.

Ask your child

How many carrots? What color are they? Who loves to eat carrots? Can you crunch like a bunny?

What your child can say or do

Three! / Orange ones. / Hop hop! / Crunch crunch.

Out in the real world

Carrots arrive whole at every salad bar and in every veggie cup — the count-three habit can ride in the lunchbox every day.

Try it together

Feed the rabbit: cut a bunny face from paper, tape it to a cup, and feed the rabbit one carrot at a time — counting each hop of the carrot into the cup. Three carrots later, the rabbit is full and so is the counter.

Understanding check

Line up four carrots or carrot cards and ask the child to give you three. Handing over exactly three — counted or grabbed — passes.

This lesson pairs with the Carrots flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.
